title_eng: A novel method for non-invasive blood pressure estimation based on continuous pulse transit time: An observational study
abstract:
Unlike traditional pulse transit time (PTT), continuous PTT (CPTT) can be used 
to calculate PTT from all samples within the cardiac cycle. It has the potential to 
be utilized for continuous blood pressure (BP) estimation. This study evaluated 
the feasibility of CPTT as a non- invasive consecutive blood pressure estimation 
method in 20 volunteers. The CPTT was calculated with a time delay in all dis-
crete samples of photoplethysmograms measured at two different body sites. BP 
was then calculated with a regression equation. For comparative evaluation, BP 
based on PTT was also estimated. Continuous blood pressure was measured using 
a non- invasive volume clamp BP monitoring device. Four types of BP measure-
ment, systolic BP (SBP), diastolic BP (DBP), mean arterial pressure (MAP), and 
pulse pressure (PP), were estimated using PTT and CPTT. Correlation coefficients 
and root- mean- squared- error (RMSE) were used for evaluating BP estimation 
performance. For estimating SBP, DBP, PP, and MAP, PTT- based BP estimation 
showed correlations of .407, .373, .410, and .286, respectively, and CPTT- based 
BP estimation showed correlations of .436, .446, .506, and .097, respectively. With 
PTT- based estimation, the RMSE between the estimated BP and the baseline BP 
was 5.44 ± 1.56 mmHg for SBP, 3.14 ± 0.46 mmHg for DBP, 3.66 ± 0.70 mmHg for 
MAP, and 3.73 ± 1.31 mmHg for PP. The estimated BP using CPTT showed RMSE 
of 5.36 ± 1.39 mmHg for SBP, 3.02 ± 0.49 mmHg for SBP, 3.44 ± 0.63 mmHg for 
MAP, and 3.91 ± 1.41 mmHg for PP.

1 | INTRODUCTION
Existing techniques such as auscultatory, oscillometry, 
volume clamp method, and arterial tonometry for non- 
invasive blood pressure (NIBP) measurement typically 
apply pressure on the human body to measure BP, which 
is inconvenient for the subject. In addition, these meth-
ods cannot be used for continuous measurement of BP 
in daily activities. Recent research on BP measurement 
has been conducted to minimize restraint of the human 
body. Cuffless BP monitoring is a generic term for all 
methods that measure blood pressure without a cuff. The 
cuffless method has the advantage of being free from 
discomfort and pain caused by using a cuff. It can also 
be used to measure blood pressure at all times in daily 
life because it does not require a complicated or bulky

Among various techniques, pulse transit time (PTT), 
which considers time difference between pulse wave ar -
rival times at two measuring sites in the human body, is 
being actively investigated. Pulse wave velocity (PWV) is 
the velocity at which pulse wave propagates between two 
points in the human body. The PWV changes with BP vari-
ations (Hickson & McSwiney, 1924), and the relationship 
between PWV and BP was theoretically proven using the 
Moens– Korteweg equation and the Bramwell and Hill 
equation (Hughes et al.,  1979). PTT is regarded as an in-
dicator of BP mediated by PWV through relationships 
such as PWV∝PTT −1 and PWV∝dP 1/2(Chen et al.,  2009; 
Ma et al.,  2018; Vlachopoulos et al.,  2011). Many stud-
ies have shown that PTT is a promising marker for BP 
measurement (Ding & Zhang,  2019; Geddes et al.,  1981; 
Gesche et al.,  2012; Huynh et al.,  2019; Kim et al.,  2015; 
Mukkamala et al.,  2015; Poon & Zhang,  2006; Smith 
et al., 1999; Wang et al., 2018; Wibmer et al., 2015).
Many of the PTT- based BP estimation studies are based 
on a regression model. To date, most algorithms have been 
developed based on linear and nonlinear regression mod-
els (Ding & Zhang, 2019). A simple linear regression model 
using PTT or PTT −1 as a single index (Mase et al.,  2011; 
Wong et al., 2009), a multiple linear regression model that 
combines PTT with heart rate and arterial stiffness index 
(Baek et al., 2009), and PTT variability as a neural control 
index have been proposed as linear regression models for 
estimating BP with PTT (Ma,  2014). In nonlinear regres -
sion model- based BP estimation research, the pulse wave 
that moves through the blood vessel is interpreted as me -
chanical energy. Therefore, the PWV corresponding to the 
velocity of the kinetic energy is considered to be the re -
ciprocal of the PTT, which is modeled as a nonlinear cor -
relation between BP and PTT (Choi et al.,  2013; Gesche 
et al.,  2012; Wibmer et al.,  2014). Recently, we have pro -
posed continuous PTT (CPTT), a method of calculating 
PTT for every sample (Shin & Choi,  2020). CPTT is cal-
culated according to the time delay in all discrete samples 
of the pulse wave measured at two different body sites. 
Therefore, unlike conventional PTT, which is only cal-
culated at a specific point in the waveform with only one 
value per pulse, it provides a PTT value at all points of the 
waveform, allowing for the pulse wave propagation time 
in a specific cardiac cycle, such as systole and diastole, to 
be calculated. Moreover, a robust measurement of CPTT 
could be derived without the preprocessing process, such 
as peak detection, which is vulnerable to noise.
The aim of this study was to determine the feasibility 
of estimating BP using CPTT as an alternative to PTT. To 
date, when estimating BP based on PTT, only one indica-
tor, PTT, has been used to estimate systolic blood pressure 
(SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP). However, it is 
not reasonable to estimate both SBP and DBP by using 
only one index independent of the cardiac cycle consid-
ering that the PWV changes with the applied pressure, 
which itself varies according to the cardiac cycle. The 
CPTT used in this study can reflect changes in PTT within 
the heartbeat cycle, enabling a more sophisticated analy -
sis for multiple types of BP estimation even without fea-
ture extraction.
2 | METHOD
2.1 | Pulse transit time and continuous 
pulse transit time
We have proposed CPTT in a previous study (Shin & 
Choi, 2020). The CPTT is characterized as having a contin-
uous value, whereas conventional PTT is calculated by the 
time difference of a specific feature like the systolic peak. 
Figure 1 shows calculation methods for PTT (Figure  1a) 
and CPTT (Figure  1b). Conventional PTT is calculated 
from the time difference between specific points of two 
PPGs measured at a distance from each other (Figure 1a). 
Here, the specific point may be a systolic peak that has a 
maximum value within a pulse, a pulse onset that has a 
minimum value within a pulse, or a maximum slope. To 
calculate PTT, a complex peak detection process should 
precede. It is derived as one value per beat. The CPTT is 
derived by calculating the delay of two signals within a 
moving window of a certain length. At this time, the signal 
delay is determined based on the point at which the cor-
relation coefficient has the maximum value by calculating 
the cross- correlation of two signals (Figure 1b). The CPTT 
can be derived without preprocessing, such as peak detec-
tion. It can be calculated for every sample. Previous stud-
ies have shown that CPTT calculated by cross- correlation 
of two PPGs differs from absolute PTT compared to con-
ventional PTT, although CPTT exhibits a similar tendency 
with a correlation coefficient of .7 or more with existing 
PTT (Shin & Choi, 2020).
2.2 | BP estimation using PTT and CPTT
2.2.1 | PTT- based BP estimation
Conventional PTT- based BP estimation methods showed 
a relatively low estimation error for SBP estimation, but 
a relatively large error for DBP estimation. This was at-
tributed to the fact that PTT was used to estimate two 
variables, SBP and DBP. Diastolic BP was estimated 
using PTT calculated on the basis of systolic features

2.2.2 | CPTT- based BP estimation
Since CPTT corresponds to a PTT that is continuously 
calculated for all cycles, including systolic and diastolic 
periods, it may reduce the estimation error accord-
ing to the heartbeat period in which PTT is extracted. 
CPTT may also improve BP estimation performance.
